This synergistic combination of electrical stimulation and controlled biochemical delivery accelerated recovery across a 10-mm sciatic defect over eight weeks, with SFI values and neural protein expression (S-100β, NF200) showing no significant difference from autograft in the reported comparisons (Fig. 6c), exemplifying a battery-free platform that unifies physical, electrical, and biochemical therapies within a single implant. Complementing this approach, Jeon et al. prioritized biomimetic structural design by arranging aligned PLLA/PEG nanofibers (20 wt% PEG; Young's modulus 128.73 MPa) into a fascicle-mimetic four-channel architecture that generated 161.2 mV (Vpp) and 58.7 nA (Ipp) under 40 kHz ultrasound [50]. The resulting APNF-NGC (aligned piezoelectric nanofiber nerve guidance conduit) enhanced axon elongation in iPSC-derived motor neurons in vitro (Fig. 6d) and achieved autograft-comparable reinnervation in an 8-mm rat sciatic defect at 12 weeks, including recovered ankle kinematics (toe-off angle: 64.4 ± 2.6°; contracture angle: 126.6 ± 3.0°) and myelinated axon counts (615 ± 49.9), demonstrating that anisotropic physical guidance and ultrasound-driven stimulation are mutually reinforcing therapeutic axes.

More recent investigations have expanded the mechanistic scope of piezoelectric nerve repair to encompass immune microenvironment modulation and next-generation biodegradable materials with exceptional electromechanical performance. A recent study by Qi et al. developed a suture-free piezoelectric Janus membrane for peripheral nerve regeneration by incorporating aligned GelMA-tannic acid fibers (GT) as the inner layer and methanol-treated silk fibroin (SF) as the outer layer in a band-aid-like fashion. The GT fibers help in tissue adhesion and directional axonal growth, while the SF layer helps in piezoelectric functionality. The membrane exhibited piezoelectric activity under mechanical activation. The fibers showed significantly enhanced PC12 neurite extension and alignment, while also exhibiting antibacterial activity of 94.3% against Staphylococcus aureus and 88.5% against Escherichia coli. In rat sciatic nerve defect model, the group with SF-GT fiber along with externally activated low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) enhanced axonal regeneration, vascularization, and motor and sensory recovery as compared to the group without stimulation. This was further supported by immunohistochemical analysis showcasing GAP43 and NCAM1 expression, especially after LIPUS activation [51]. Ding et al., in 2025 fabricated a laser-additively manufactured PLLA scaffold incorporating Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets and UIO-66 MOF nanoparticles (Fig. 6e), wherein ultrasonic stimulation exploited the synergy between UIO-66-generated piezoelectric potential and MXene's charge-transfer efficiency to produce a stable peak current of 0.036 μA. This output drove macrophage M1-to-M2 polarization (CD206+ cells: 91.02% vs. 78.15% in PLLA controls) by upregulating ATP-sensitive K+ channels and suppressing the Ca2+-CaMKII-NF-κB axis via VGCC downregulation, while simultaneously promoting BMSC neuronal differentiation (Tuj1 and MAP2 upregulation) in an inflammatory environment, supporting an in vitro immune-related mechanism; this study did not establish functional repair in an animal nerve-gap model. Extending the material frontier, Dai et al., in 2026 embedded Rochelle salt micro-crystals within electrospun PLLA nanofibers and applied uniaxial compression to yield a biodegradable composite (PRSC, Fig. 6f) with a d33eff of 43.1 ± 3.0 pC N−1 and g33 of 1909.2 mV m N−1 [29], surpassing all previously reported biodegradable flexible piezoelectrics [85,117,118]. In a 10-mm rat sciatic defect model, ultrasound-activated PRSC scaffolds achieved an axon length of 7.53 ± 0.18 mm and SFI recovery without a significant difference from autograft in the reported comparisons by modulating intracellular calcium via Cav3.2 channels and upregulating Gap43 and Galanin. Beyond nerve repair, the same material platform functioned as a biodegradable strain sensor (sensitivity: 0.049 ± 0.003 V kPa−1) for real-time wireless monitoring of intestinal motility, illustrating the broader translational potential of high-performance biodegradable piezoelectrics across neuromodulation and physiological sensing applications. The key material parameters, stimulation strategies, and in vivo outcomes of these wireless externally activated piezoelectric systems are collectively summarized in Table 5.

Collectively, these studies highlight the rapid technological evolution of piezoelectric electroceutical platforms for nerve regeneration, progressing from early motion-responsive scaffolds that generate endogenous electrical cues, to advanced composite materials with enhanced electrical output, and ultimately to remotely activated acousto-piezoelectric systems capable of delivering externally adjustable electrical stimulation whose delivered dose still requires measurement and multifunctional therapeutic effects. This progression underscores the growing potential of self-powered bioelectronic scaffolds to bridge critical nerve gaps, modulate the regenerative microenvironment, and provide next-generation strategies for peripheral nerve repair.

Three decades of incremental progress in passive nerve conduits have yielded a frustrating ceiling: hollow tubes and collagen scaffolds reliably bridge short gaps but consistently fail to restore the electrophysiological fidelity that meaningful motor and sensory recovery demands. The past decade's pivot toward self-powered bioelectronic neuromodulation has fundamentally reframed this problem, shifting the design question from “how do we guide axons?” to “how do we recreate the endogenous bioelectric landscape that drives regeneration?” Galvanic cells, triboelectric nanogenerators, and piezoelectric nanogenerators each represent a distinct answer to that question, and their comparative strengths and limitations now define the frontier of the field.

Of the three strategies, self-electrified galvanic devices offer a relatively simple strategy for movement-independent postoperative stimulation. They require no patient compliance, no external hardware, and no activity-dependent mechanical deformation. They simply activate upon contact with physiological fluids and deliver continuous DC stimulation while reactants and electrical continuity remain available. This simplicity is also their most significant constraint: output profile, stimulation duration, and degradation kinetics are largely fixed by material choice at the time of fabrication, leaving little room for post-implantation adjustment [119,120]. The transition from magnesium-to zinc-based anodes has meaningfully extended operational windows and reduced hydrogen evolution, and architectures that couple galvanic stimulation with integrated neural recording provide a basis for future responsive therapy, but recording alone does not establish a closed loop. Nevertheless, the field has yet to demonstrate reliable stimulation delivery calibrated to the weeks-long regeneration timeline in large-animal or human nerve injury contexts, and this remains the central translational bottleneck.

TENGs occupy an intriguing middle ground. They can generate substantially higher voltages than galvanic cells and are inherently synchronized with the patient's own physiological movements, creating physiologically coupled neuromodulation rather than validated therapeutic feedback. Their susceptibility to output variability under immobilization, however, is a practical limitation that restricts their applicability precisely in the acute postoperative phase when stimulation is most critical [4,11,24,26,121]. Hybrid [85] TENG-PENG architectures and acoustically triggered transient devices have begun to address this vulnerability, but the engineering complexity of ensuring stable, therapeutically adequate output across diverse patient activity levels remains unresolved. The most compelling near-term trajectory for TENGs may lie not in isolated nerve repair applications, but in their integration into wearable or partially implantable systems that simultaneously harvest energy from broader body kinematics, including respiratory motion and gait cycles, while delivering targeted stimulation to peripheral injury sites.

PENGs, particularly those that combine ultrasound activation with aligned nanofiber scaffolds, offer versatile options for activation and scaffold design. Driving piezoelectric output externally via ultrasound can reduce the immobilization constraint that limits both TENGs and motion-dependent PENGs, while allowing adjustment of the external activation settings. The recent emergence of fully biodegradable piezoelectric composites with performance metrics approaching those of non-degradable materials marks a materials science inflection point: for the first time, high-output, bioresorbable piezoelectric scaffolds are within reach, offering alternatives to PVDF-containing scaffolds while leaving long-term degradation-product safety to be established. This mechanistic insight that ultrasound-driven piezoelectric stimulation modulates intracellular calcium through defined channel subtypes rather than through a diffuse or poorly characterized pathway, which also provides a rational basis for stimulus parameter optimization that has been largely absent from earlier empirical approaches.

Looking forward, the convergence of these three technologies within integrated, multifunctional platforms may ultimately prove more powerful than any single strategy pursued in isolation. A device architecture that combines the sustained baseline stimulation of a galvanic cell with the on-demand, adjustable output of an acoustically activated piezoelectric layer—while incorporating real-time electrophysiological recording—addresses the full temporal arc of peripheral nerve regeneration. Advances in biodegradable soft electronics, machine learning-assisted signal processing, and biofabrication may enable such closed-loop bio-electroceuticals, but clinical validation remains necessary (Fig. 7). Realizing this translational roadmap will require continued materials innovation, standardized preclinical evaluation frameworks, and regulatory pathways tailored for devices whose functional lifetime is intentionally finite. Ultimately, the foundational science reviewed here establishes that self-powered electrical stimulation can meaningfully accelerate nerve repair; the work ahead lies in translating that proof of concept into a reliable, clinically deployable therapy.

Despite encouraging preclinical results, clinical translation of self-powered bioelectronic devices for peripheral nerve regeneration remains limited: most galvanic devices, TENGs, and PENGs have been validated only in small-animal models, with little evidence for long-term performance under clinically relevant anatomical and biomechanical conditions. Translation will require reproducible electrical output, stable therapeutic performance throughout the intended treatment period, predictable material degradation, and validation in large-animal models (pig, sheep, non-human primate) to establish implant stability, anatomical fit, and chronic immune response ahead of first-in-human study [41,122,123].

Biological evaluation of biodegradable bioelectronic devices should follow ISO 10993 [124] at the whole-device level, thereby addressing degradation products, residual materials, sterilization effects, electrical safety, and long-term functionality, rather than individual material properties in isolation. Externally activated systems additionally require systematic validation of acoustic exposure, thermal effects, cavitation, and stimulation reproducibility under clinically relevant conditions [115,[125], [126], [127]]. Beyond biological safety, translation depends on establishing standardized stimulation-dose benchmarks that correlate electrical parameters (current density, charge density, pulse width, frequency, treatment duration) with molecular, histological, electrophysiological, and functional outcomes a framework that would allow direct comparison across galvanic, triboelectric, and piezoelectric platforms and thereby accelerate regulatory approval and commercialization [41,[128], [129], [130]].

sections.title: Chronic inflammation, material fate, and large-animal validation

paragraphs.en: All implantable biodegradable bioelectronic devices still elicit a foreign body response that can compromise host and immune responses [131]. Protein adsorption, acute and chronic inflammation, macrophage activation, foreign body giant cell (FBGC) production, fibroblast recruitment, and fibrotic capsule creation are the successive stages of the foreign body response. Excessive fibrosis and collagen deposition increase the distance between the electrode and regenerating nerve tissues, elevating electrical impedance and lowering stimulation efficiency. Therefore, long term evaluation should include serial assessment of macrophage phenotype, FBGC formation, fibrotic capsule thickness, electrophysiology, local tissue microenvironment, degradation, and systemic clearance. Short-term cytocompatibility or a single organ-histology time point cannot establish long-term safety. Studies should span implantation, active treatment, loss of function, maximum degradation burden, and subsequent clearance or stable retention.

Galvanic nerve stimulators, especially Mg, Zn, FeMn, Mo, and Si containing systems, are primarily limited by electrochemical degradation. Local corrosion, pH elevation, gas generation, and systemic distribution may influence macrophage recruitment and tissue compatibility [132]. Consequently, degradation kinetics, electrochemical stability, and systemic clearance should be evaluated to minimize chronic inflammation while maintaining stable electrical output. In TENGs, chronic inflammation is largely associated with repeated mechanical deformation, micromotion at the implant-tissue interface, and incomplete degradation of structural polymers or conductive materials. These contribute to sustained macrophage activation and promote fibrotic remodelling and escalate collagen capsule thickness, thereby reducing electrical coupling between the device and regenerating nerve tissue [133]. Moreover, in PENGs, chronic inflammatory responses are governed by the incomplete degradation profile of piezo polymers and fillers. Biodegradable polymers such as silk fibroin, PLLA, and PLGA exhibit good mechanical compatibility, incomplete degradation or prolonged retention of PVDF, PDMS, persistent conductors, and ceramic or carbon-based fillers in the surrounding matrix may sustain macrophage activation, inflammasome signaling, and fibrotic encapsulation. Therefore, biological evaluation should include complete assessment of device degradation, systemic clearance, and long-term tissue compatibility using a risk-based framework [132].

Large-animal validation remains a major translational gap for bioelectronic devices: galvanic, TENGs, and PENGs technologies. Transmission through excised porcine/rabbit/ tissue is not equivalent to regeneration in a living large-animal nerve. Most studies have been performed in rodent models, which do not adequately reproduce clinically relevant nerve diameter, regeneration distance, delayed repair and movement, chronic inflammation, or immune responses encountered in humans. Consequently, the long-term electrical performance studies should be performed to understand the degradation behavior, chronic inflammation, fibrotic encapsulation, and material fate of these devices following established standard protocol (ISO10993) [124]. Future models should reflect clinically relevant nerve dimensions, delayed repair, and physiological movement, and include autograft and matched non-stimulating controls. Outcome measures should combine motor and sensory recovery, muscle force, electrophysiology, nerve organization, chronic inflammatory responses, degradation, and systemic clearance of implanted materials. A proposed 6-12 month observation period may be appropriate for some models, with extension for slow degradation or retained components; this is a development target, rather than a universal regulatory requirement.

Closed-loop bioelectronic systems represent the next generation of neural interfaces by integrating energy harvesting, sensing, signal processing, and adaptive stimulation into a single autonomous platform. A therapeutic closed loop requires a measured variable, a target or decision rule, an actuator that changes stimulation, and evidence that this adjustment improves dose control or outcome; physiological coupling and simultaneous neural recording, as in FI-NES and Bio-Restor, do not establish that complete loop. Candidate feedback variables include delivered current/charge, electrode impedance, evoked compound muscle action potential (CMAP), mechanical deformation at the electrode–tissue interface, and other validated neural responses [52,134]. Impedance monitoring is highly sensitive to interface changes but is not a specific measure of nerve regeneration. Practical implementation additionally requires stimulation-artifact rejection, defined sensing intervals, bounded energy budgets, and safe shutdown during signal loss or excessive polarization. The engineering solution is platform-specific: ultrasound-driven systems can adjust burst timing or source intensity, whereas galvanic systems require added switching or current-limiting hardware. Validation should directly compare open-loop and feedback-controlled treatment under matched resources, including disturbances and progressive degradation, to establish whether adaptive control meaningfully improves outcomes.

Future biodegradable bioelectronic platforms aim to combine self-powered energy harvesting, multimodal sensing, wireless communication, and adaptive stimulation within a single implantable device. Realizing this will require low-power sensing electronics, robust artifact rejection, and energy-efficient control algorithms operating within the limited power budget of biodegradable self-powered systems. Candidate technologies include galvanic self-powered stimulators, triboelectric and piezoelectric nanogenerators, ultrasound-mediated neuromodulation, and magnetoelectric interfaces. Translation will require systematic improvement in material biodegradability, electrical performance, and closed-loop control algorithms, progressing from in vitro and small-animal studies to validation in clinically relevant large-animal models, with attention to implantation stability, immune response, degradation behavior, and long-term wireless communication reliability. Achieving this alongside scalable manufacturing and regulatory compliance would allow biodegradable electroceuticals to mature into minimally invasive, energy-autonomous platforms for precision peripheral nerve regeneration.

The schematic illustrates the bioengineering-to-clinical-practice pipeline for self-powered bioelectronics in peripheral nerve regeneration. Peripheral nervous system injury impairs neural connections, which leads to clinical disorders such as cardiac rhythm abnormalities, bronchoconstriction, axonal degeneration, and demyelination. To overcome conventional therapy limitations, self-powered electroceutical platforms integrate biodegradable electroactive materials that will effectively produce implantable bioelectronic devices capable of generating therapeutic electrical stimulation.

The roadmap begins with the selective electroactive materials selection, including biodegradable metals, polymers, ceramics, and conductive fibers, which determine the electrical, mechanical, and degradation characteristics of the device. The implantable materials are engineered as galvanic, triboelectric, piezoelectric, and hybrid nerve guidance conduits, where material composition, device architecture, and energy-transduction mechanisms collectively regulate electrical output and stimulation duration by converting endogenous electrochemical or biomechanical energy into therapeutic electrical output. Clinically optimized electrical cues will activate multiple regenerative processes, including Schwann cell activation, axonal elongation, remyelination, angiogenesis, neuromuscular junction formation, and modulation of inflammatory responses, ultimately promoting functional peripheral nerve regeneration. At the translational level, biodegradable self-powered platforms offer several potential clinical advantages, including battery-free operation, minimally invasive implantation, elimination of secondary removal surgery, and personalized neuromodulation.
